title: The Unsolved Mystery Disappearance of the Sodder Children
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the unsolved disappearance of the Sodder children, a Fayetteville, West Virginia family whose five youngest children vanished after their house burned on Christmas Eve/morning 1945 (the episode says 1945 implicitly via context of WWII; the children were never found). They cover George Sodder's immigration from Sardinia and his trucking business, his outspoken anti-Mussolini views, the Christmas Eve night events (a strange phone call, a thump on the roof), the fire and slow fire department response, the buried site and later excavations, the Smithsonian report on vertebrae, the fake heart hoax, numerous sightings and tips, the Lewis Sodder photo letter, the billboard, the mafia theory, and Sylvia as last surviving sibling. The episode ends with listener mail from Sean about lead chromate in road paint and a sign-off mention of a Karen Abbott article and an NPR piece by Stacy Horn.

segments.title: Live show announcement and Square Space sponsor read
segments.summary: Sponsor read for Squarespace and announcement of upcoming live shows in Boston and Washington, D.C., with ticket details.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the unsolved mystery episode about the Sodder family of Fayetteville, West Virginia, and Josh mentions a texted exchange with Justin McElroy about a local billboard.

segments.title: George Sodder's immigration and trucking business
segments.summary: George Sodder arrives from Sardinia as a teenager, works for the Pennsylvania Railroad, moves to Smithers and then Fayetteville, and builds a middle-class trucking business hauling coal and dirt. The family is well respected in a small Italian community.

segments.title: Anti-Mussolini views and local arguments
segments.summary: George is outspoken against Mussolini during WWII and gets into arguments with locals who disagree.

segments.title: Christmas Eve and the mysterious phone call
segments.summary: The family opens gifts on Christmas Eve, and the five younger children stay up playing with new toys. Around midnight, Jenny answers a phone call from a woman asking for someone unknown, with a party audible in the background. Jenny checks the house, leaves a sleeping child on the couch, and later hears a thump on the roof.

segments.title: The house fire and rescue attempts
segments.summary: The house catches fire. Parents and older children escape with Sylvia, but five children are trapped upstairs. George cuts his arm trying to re-enter, the staircase is engulfed, and he tries to use a ladder and trucks, which fail to start. The ladder is later reported stolen. The house burns in roughly forty-five minutes.

segments.title: Delayed fire department response and no remains found
segments.summary: Neighbors struggle to reach the fire department because no operator is on duty and there is no siren, so they use a phone tree. The fire truck arrives around eight a.m. to find ash. No remains of the five children are found, and George buries the site with fill dirt.

segments.title: Suspicious warnings, threats, and sightings
segments.summary: The family recounts odd details: a stranger warned about wiring, a life insurance salesman who threatened them over Mussolini comments, a parked van watching the children, and the coroner's inquest ruling of faulty wiring. Later, the family pursues searches, excavations, a Smithsonian report on bone fragments, and the fake heart hoax.

segments.title: Lewis Sodder photo letter, billboard, and theories
segments.summary: The family receives tips and sightings across the country, including a Houston lead and a photo postmarked Kentucky. J. Edgar Hoover's FBI offers help only if local police invite it. The family erects a billboard offering a reward, and theories include the mafia. Sylvia, the last surviving sibling, keeps the story alive.

segments.title: Listener mail on lead paint in road markings
segments.summary: Listener Sean writes that roadside signs generally do not use lead paint, though lead chromate may remain in some older road markings. The hosts discuss the message.

segments.title: Sign-off and further reading
segments.summary: Hosts recommend a Karen Abbott article and a Stacy Horn NPR piece and sign off.
